True Statement: As per WHO, health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease.
False 1: As per WHO, health is defined as the complete absence of disease in the body.
False 2: As per WHO, health is defined as a state of complete physical well-being only.

True Statement: A symptom is what we feel (like pain or tiredness), while a sign is something that can be seen or measured (like fever or rash).
False 1: A sign is what we feel (like pain or tiredness), while a symptom is something that can be seen or measured (like fever or rash).

True Statement: A disease is a condition that affects the normal working of the body or mind, when one or more organs or organ systems stop functioning properly.
False 1: A disease only affects the body, not the mind.

True Statement: Disease-causing organisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms, and protozoa) are called pathogens.
False 1: Disease-causing organisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms, and algae) are called pathogens.

True Statement: Non-communicable diseases (such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma) are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from one person to another; they are linked to lifestyle, diet, and environment.
False 1: Communicable diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from person to person.
False 2: Non-communicable diseases like cancer and diabetes are caused by bacteria and viruses but cannot spread from person to person.

True Statement: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread from one person to another (e.g., typhoid, dengue, flu, chickenpox, COVID-19).
False 1: Non-communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and spread from one person to another.

True Statement: Today, most deaths in India are caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs).
False 1: Today, most deaths in India are caused by communicable diseases.

True Statement: Common cold and influenza are caused by a virus; their site of infection is the respiratory tract.
False 1: Common cold and influenza are caused by bacteria.
False 2: Common cold and influenza are caused by a virus; their site of infection is the intestine.

True Statement: Chickenpox is caused by a virus; it affects the respiratory tract and skin; symptoms include mild fever, itchy skin, rashes, and blisters.
False 1: Chickenpox is caused by bacteria.
False 2: Chickenpox is caused by a virus; it affects the intestine; symptoms include diarrhoea and dehydration.

True Statement: Measles is caused by a virus; symptoms include fever, sore throat, and reddish rashes on the neck, ears, and other parts of the skin.
False 1: Measles is caused by bacteria.
False 2: Measles is caused by a virus; symptoms include diarrhoea and dehydration.

True Statement: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by bacteria and affects the lungs; symptoms include cough, fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, and night sweats.
False 1: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a virus.
False 2: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by bacteria and affects the intestine.

True Statement: Hepatitis A is caused by a virus and affects the liver; symptoms include fatigue, fever, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice.
False 1: Hepatitis A is caused by bacteria.
False 2: Hepatitis A is caused by a virus and affects the intestine.

True Statement: Cholera is caused by bacteria and affects the intestine; its symptoms are diarrhoea and dehydration.
False 1: Cholera is caused by a virus.
False 2: Cholera is caused by bacteria and affects the liver.

True Statement: Typhoid is caused by bacteria and affects the intestine; symptoms include headache, abdominal discomfort, fever, and diarrhoea.
False 1: Typhoid is caused by a virus.
False 2: Typhoid is caused by bacteria and affects the liver.

True Statement: Ascariasis (roundworms) is caused by worms and affects the intestine; symptoms include worms in stool, loss of appetite, poor growth, diarrhoea, weight loss, and anaemia.
False 1: Ascariasis is caused by bacteria.
False 2: Ascariasis is caused by worms and affects the skin and blood.

True Statement: Malaria is caused by protozoa and affects the skin and blood; symptoms include high fever, profuse sweating, and periodic chills.
False 1: Malaria is caused by a virus.

True Statement: Dengue fever (Break bone fever) is caused by a virus and affects the skin and blood; symptoms include fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, and nausea.
False 1: Dengue fever is caused by bacteria.
False 2: Dengue fever is caused by a virus; its symptoms include diarrhoea and dehydration.

True Statement: Vectors are insects (such as mosquitoes and houseflies) that spread pathogens from one person to another.
False 1: Vectors are pathogens that enter the body through contaminated food and water.

True Statement: Deficiency diseases (such as scurvy, anaemia, and goitre) are caused by lack of specific nutrients in the diet and are non-communicable.
False 1: Deficiency diseases are caused by pathogens.
False 2: Deficiency diseases are communicable and spread from person to person.

True Statement: Chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma may persist for more than 3 months.
False 1: Chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and asthma may persist for more than 3 weeks.

True Statement: Diabetes often develops due to hormonal imbalances, unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity, and being overweight or obese.
False 1: Diabetes is caused by pathogens like bacteria or viruses.

True Statement: Immunity is the natural ability of the body to fight diseases; the immune system helps fight against pathogens.
False 1: Immunity is the body's inability to fight diseases.

True Statement: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs, providing acquired immunity — protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or vaccine.
False 1: Vaccines provide natural immunity that is present from birth.
False 2: Vaccines are curative — they can treat disease even after someone is already sick.

True Statement: Vaccines can be made from weakened or dead pathogens, or from inactive or harmless parts of the pathogen.
False 1: Vaccines are made from living, fully active pathogens.

True Statement: In the late 1700s, Edward Jenner discovered that people who had cowpox did not get smallpox, leading to the first vaccine.
False 1: In the late 1700s, Alexander Fleming discovered that people who had cowpox did not get smallpox, leading to the first vaccine.
False 2: In the late 1700s, Louis Pasteur discovered that cowpox infection protects against smallpox.

True Statement: India had a traditional method called variolation to protect against smallpox, involving material from a smallpox sore to create mild infection and build immunity; practitioners were called teekedaars.
False 1: India's traditional smallpox practitioners (teekedaars) used material from cowpox sores, not smallpox sores, to build immunity.

True Statement: Vaccines are preventive, not curative — they help minimise serious diseases before they happen but do not treat them once someone is already sick.
False 1: Vaccines are curative — they treat a disease after someone is already infected.

True Statement: Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections; they do not work against viruses or diseases caused by protozoa.
False 1: Antibiotics work against all types of infections including viruses.
False 2: Antibiotics work only against viral infections and do not work against bacterial infections.

True Statement: Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming, who noticed that a mould on a discarded petri dish stopped bacteria from growing.
False 1: Penicillin was discovered by Edward Jenner after noticing a mould that stopped bacteria from growing.
False 2: Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming, who noticed that a mould killed viruses.

True Statement: Antibiotic resistance is a phenomenon where bacteria that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic survive and multiply despite treatment with that antibiotic.
False 1: Antibiotic resistance is a phenomenon where viruses that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic survive and multiply.

True Statement: To prevent antibiotic resistance, antibiotics should be used only when prescribed by a doctor, in the correct dose, and for the right duration.
False 1: To prevent antibiotic resistance, antibiotics should be taken frequently and in high doses to kill all bacteria completely.
